title: Colonial Terminals - Austell
current_scope:
Purpose of Application On January 27, 2026, CTOC submitted Application No. 30031 requesting a Synthetic Minor (SM) permit to replace the current permit No. 5171-067-0274-E-01-0. In the application, the facility is requesting the existing federally enforceable limits on fuel throughputs and on emissions from the loading rack to be

Page 2: SIP Application Review Colonial Terminals Operating Company LLC Austell Terminal, Application No. 30031 Page 2 of 17 maintained to ensure applicable Title V and NESHAP major source thresholds are not exceeded. I n addition, the application does not propose any changes in the production process or equipment. Therefore, there will be no potential VOC emission increase s associated with Application No. 30031. The application was accepted into EPD’s Expedited Permitting Program on February 6, 2026. According to Application No. 30031, as guided by relevant EPA policy memos, CTOC has re-evaluated its source status and relation ship to the nearby Colonial Pipeline Company (CPC) - Atlanta Junction pipeline breakout facility (AIRS No. 067-00074) under pertinent NSR and Title V rules, and believed that CTOC and CPC Atlanta Junction are two separate facilities for Title V and NSR permitting purposes for the reasons below: First, while two facilities are physically adjacent, they belong to different SIC Code Major Groupings. CTOC operates in Major Group 51 (Wholesale trade -nondurable goods) , but CPC – Atlanta Junction operates in Major Group 46 (Pipelines, except natural gas). Second, EPA guidance has consistently indicated that “control” means having “authority that exercises restraining or directing influence over a source’s economic or other relevant, pollutant emitting activities”1. In this case, the ultimate owner of CTOC and CPC -Atlanta Junction does not exercise restraining or directing influence over both CPC’s and CTOC – Atlanta Junction’s economic activities. Regulations promulgated by the Interstate Commerce Act (“ICA”) are governing the interstate transportation of oil and related commodities, as engaged by CPC -Atlanta Junction. Regulation under the ICA grants the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) distinct jurisdiction over and imposes strict restrictions on interstate transportation providers (a.k.a. common carriers), including their economic activities, to ensure fair and non -discriminatory access to the pipeline network. As such, CPC - Atlanta Junction is considered to be FERC -jurisdictional under the ICA, whereas CTOC and its economic activities are not subject to FERC jurisdiction and ICA regulation. Third, US EPA has further clarified the issue of common control in a 2018 letter 2 . EPA stated “Ultimately, the focus is not on how control is established (through ownership, contract, or otherwise), but on whether control is established —that is, whether one entity can expressly or effectively force another entity to take a specific course of action, which the other entity cannot avoid through its own independent decision-making.” In this case, FERC/ICA regulations and the implementing policies within CPC ownership prevent CPC -Atlanta Junction and CTOC from expressly or effectively forcing the other entity to take a specific course of action. Fourth, the fact that there is a contractual relationship between CPC - Atlanta Junction and CTOC does not necessarily indicate common control. The contractual relationship has been negotiated at arm’s length in alignment with FERC/ICA regulatory requirements. Per the 2018 EPA letter (Ref. Footnote 2), “…the fact that an entity is influenced, affected, or somewhat constrained by contractual relationships that it negotiated at arm’s length, or by external market forces, does not necessarily mean that one entity is actually controlled or governed by these influences in making a given decision.” Since CPC - Atlanta Junction and CPC are governed independently regarding operational functions and regulatory requirements, these two facilities are not under common control and should be treated as separate facilities with respect to Title V and PSD major source permitting. 1 Major Source Determinations for Military Installations under the Air Toxics, New Source Review, and Title V Operating Permit Programs of the Clean Air Act. title: South Atlanta Asphalt Plant
current_scope: Purpose of Application The Permittee submitted a SIP Permit Amendment Application assigned Application No. 30323 on September 11, 2026, for replacing the existing permitted drum dryer and baghouse with a like-kind new drum dryer and baghouse since the existing dryer is unable to produce more than 300 tons/day of hot mix asphalt. A permit advisory was issued for this permit application.
